subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
passage:
At home, the night before the school concert:
Rashmi: Trisha, sing me the whole song.
Trisha: Okay. Golden fields, silver rain... (she sings the first verse beautifully).
Rashmi: Now the second verse.
Trisha: Later, Amma. Let me do the first one again. I like it best.
The next day, backstage:
Trisha: I nailed the first verse! But then... Amma, the second verse just went. My mind was blank. I hummed and stood there.
Rashmi: I saw. Everyone heard the pause.
Trisha: I only practised the part I liked. The rest I barely touched.

qa.q: Which verse did Trisha keep practising at home?
qa.a: Trisha kept practising the first verse.

qa.q: What might Trisha feel backstage after forgetting the second verse?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels embarrassed and disappointed, since the blank and the humming happened in front of everyone. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Trisha use next time, and why?
qa.a: Trisha could give the hardest or least known parts the most practice, or sing the whole song from the start each time. That way every verse is ready on the stage.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see the concert moment?
qa.a: Rashmi saw and heard the pause, and answers gently, so Rashmi probably feels sympathetic and wants Trisha to learn from it without being blamed.

grounding: A girl keeps repeating the first verse she enjoys, and on stage she forgets the second verse she has barely practised.

subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
passage: Our school choir sang at the district festival last month, and I had a solo, two verses. I loved the first verse. It had a high note that made my arms tingle, so I sang it everywhere: in the bath, walking to school, while Amma cooked. The second verse was harder, so I kept thinking, "Later." My little brother Hrithik even knew verse one by heart and sang it back to me. On the day I walked out and sang verse one perfectly. Then the music went on, and my mouth opened, and nothing was there. Rukmini, the girl who knew every note of verse one, stood in silence. The choir teacher started singing with me. My face burned all afternoon.

qa.q: Who knew verse one by heart and sang it back to Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini's little brother Hrithik knew verse one by heart.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel when the second verse was not there?
qa.a: Rukmini felt shocked and deeply embarrassed, with a burning face all afternoon.

qa.q: What would you change first in Rukmini's practice, and why?
qa.a: Practise the hard second verse first each day, because the part you avoid is the part most likely to break under pressure.

qa.q: How might the moment have looked to the choir teacher?
qa.a: The choir teacher saw a strong start and then silence, and quickly sang along to help; it was probably a worried moment.

grounding: It shows a girl practising only the verse she enjoys, being confident at first on stage and then forgetting the second verse she barely practised.

subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
passage:
Music teacher's note, after the inter-house singing
Preeti's first verse today was the best I've heard from her. She had clearly practised it many times; she even closed her eyes on the long note. Then the second verse began, and she stopped. She looked at me with wide eyes, and I mouthed the first words. She caught up halfway through, quietly. Afterwards she told me she had sung verse one "a hundred times" because she loved it, and verse two only twice. She was very upset. I told her the slip did not undo the lovely first verse. From next week, our practice rule will be: start with the verse you know least. I have told Irfan, her house captain, too.
- Music teacher

qa.q: How many times did Preeti say she sang verse two?
qa.a: She said she sang verse two only twice.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel after the song?
qa.a: She was very upset about stopping, even though her first verse was lovely.

qa.q: What other approach would suit Preeti better, and why?
qa.a: Starting practice with the verse she knows least, because it gives the weak part the most attention.

qa.q: How might the slip look to Irfan, her house captain?
qa.a: Irfan might be disappointed for the house, but can also see a clear fix for next time.

grounding: It shows a girl who practised only the verse she liked, starting well on stage and then forgetting the barely practised second verse.
